The vast majority of Bolivians are mestizo (with the indigenous component higher than the European one[citation needed]), although the government has not included the cultural self-identification "mestizo" in the November 2012 census.[206] There are approximately three dozen native groups totaling approximately half of the population – the largest proportion of indigenous people in the Americas. A 2009 estimate of racial classification put mestizo (mixed White and Amerindian) at 68%, indigenous at 20%, white at 5%, cholo at 2%, black at 1%, other at 4%, while 2% were unspecified; 44% attributed themselves to some indigenous group, predominantly the linguistic categories of Quechuas or Aymaras.[207] White Bolivians comprised about 14% of the population in 2006. The ancestry of whites and the white ancestry of mestizos lies within Europe and the Middle East, most notably Spain, Italy, Germany, Croatia, Lebanon and Syria. In the Santa Cruz Department, there are several dozen colonies of German-speaking Mennonites from Russia totaling around 40,000 inhabitants (as of 2012).[208] There are around 140,000 Mennonites in Bolivia of Frisian, Flemish and German ethnic origins.[209][210]

Afro-Bolivians, descendants of African slaves who arrived in the time of the Spanish Empire, inhabit the department of La Paz and are located mainly in the provinces of Nor Yungas and Sud Yungas. Slavery was abolished in Bolivia in 1831.[211] There are also important communities of Japanese (14,000[212]) and Lebanese (12,900[213]).

Indigenous peoples, also called "originarios" ("native" or "original") and less frequently, Amerindians, could be categorized by geographic area, such as Andean, like the Aymaras and Quechuas (who formed the ancient Inca Empire), who are concentrated in the western departments of La Paz, Potosí, Oruro, Cochabamba and Chuquisaca. There also are ethnic populations in the east, composed of the Chiquitano, Chané, Guaraní and Moxos, among others, who inhabit the departments of Santa Cruz, Beni, Tarija and Pando.

There are small numbers of European citizens from Germany, France, Italy and Portugal, as well as from other countries of the Americas, as Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Cuba, Ecuador, the United States, Paraguay, Peru, Mexico and Venezuela, among others. There are important Peruvian colonies in La Paz, El Alto and Santa Cruz de la Sierra.

Languageedit
Main article: Languages of Bolivia

Bolivia has great linguistic diversity as a result of its multiculturalism. The constitution recognizes 36 official languages besides Spanish.[214] Spanish is the most spoken official language in the country, according to the 2001 census; as it is spoken by two-thirds of the population. All legal and official documents issued by the state, including the constitution, the main private and public institutions, the media, and commercial activities, are in Spanish. The main indigenous languages of the population above 4 years old are: Quechua (13.1% of the population in the 2024 census), Aymara (7.3%), Guarani (0.4%) and others (0.4%) including the Moxos in the department of Beni.[207] Plautdietsch, a German dialect, is spoken by about 70,000 Mennonites in Santa Cruz. Portuguese is spoken mainly in the areas close to Brazil.

Religionedit
Main article: Religion in Bolivia
Basilica of San Francisco in La Paz

Bolivia is a constitutionally secular state that guarantees the freedom of religion and the independence of government from religion.[215] According to the 2001 census, 78% of the population is Roman Catholic, followed by 19% that are Protestant, as well as a small number of Orthodox Christians, and 3% non-religious.[216][217]

The Association of Religion Data Archives (relying on the World Christian Database) records that in 2010, 92.5% of Bolivians identified as Christian (of any denomination), 3.1% identified with indigenous religion, 2.2% identified as Baháʼí, 1.9% identified as agnostic, and all other groups constituted 0.1% or less.[218]

Much of the indigenous population adheres to different traditional beliefs marked by inculturation or syncretism with Christianity. The cult of Pachamama,[219] or "Mother Earth", is notable. The veneration of the Virgin of Copacabana, Virgin of Urkupiña and Virgin of Socavón, is also an important feature of Christian pilgrimage. There are important Aymaran communities near Lake Titicaca that have a strong devotion to James the Apostle.[220] Deities worshiped in Bolivia include Ekeko, the Aymaran god of abundance and prosperity, whose day is celebrated every 24 January, and Tupá, a god of the Guaraní people.

Educationedit
Main article: Education in Bolivia
The Universidad Mayor Real y Pontificia San Francisco Xavier de Chuquisaca, Bolivia's oldest higher education institution

In 2008, following UNESCO standards, Bolivia was declared free of illiteracy.[221] Public and private universities include: Universidad Mayor, Real y Pontificia de San Francisco Xavier de Chuquisaca, Sucre; Universidad Mayor de San Andrés, La Paz; Universidad Mayor de San Simon, Cochabamba; Universidad Autónoma Gabriel René Moreno, Santa Cruz de la Sierra; Universidad Técnica de Oruro, Oruro; Universidad Evangélica Boliviana, Santa Cruz de la Sierra; and Universidad Autónoma Tomás Frías, Potosi.

Healthedit
Main article: Health in Bolivia
See also: Refresh Bolivia

According to UNICEF, the under-five mortality rate was 26 per 1,000[222] and the infant mortality rate was 21.1 per 1,000[223] in 2019. Before Morales took office, nearly half of all infants were not vaccinated; now nearly all are vaccinated. Morales also put into place several supplemental nutrition programs, including an effort to supply free food in public health and social security offices, and his desnutrición cero (zero malnutrition) program provides free school lunches.[159]

Between 2006 and 2016, extreme poverty fell from 38.2% to 16.8%. Chronic malnutrition in children under five years of age also went down by 14%, and the child mortality rate was reduced by more than 50%, according to World Health Organization.[224] In 2019 the government created a universal healthcare system which has been cited as a model for all by the World Health Organization.[225]

Women's rightsedit

Bolivia has one of the highest rates of femicide and gender-based violence in Latin America.[226] In 2013, the Comprehensive Law to Guarantee Women a Life Free from Violence was passed, which codifies 16 types of gender-based violence and implements measures for prevention of violence, protection for victims, and the punishment of aggressors.

As of 2022, 46% of parliamentary seats are held by women.[227] A 1997 law established quotas whereby candidates for public office fielded by political parties must be at least 30% women.[228]

Cultureedit
See also: Music of Bolivia and Public holidays in Bolivia
Gate of the Sun, 500–950 CE, Tiwanaku

Bolivian culture has been heavily influenced by the Spanish, the Aymara, and the Quechua, as well as the popular cultures of Latin America as a whole. The cultural development is divided into three distinct periods: precolumbian, colonial, and republican. Important archaeological ruins, gold and silver ornaments, stone monuments, ceramics, and weavings remain from several important pre-Columbian cultures. Major ruins include Tiwanaku, El Fuerte de Samaipata, Inkallaqta and Iskanwaya. The country abounds in other sites that are difficult to reach and have seen little archaeological exploration.[229]

The Diablada, dance primeval, typical and main of Carnival of Oruro, a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity since 2001

The Spanish brought their own tradition of religious art which, in the hands of local native, mestizo and some criollo builders and artisans, developed into a rich and distinctive style of architecture, painting, and sculpture known as Andean Baroque. The colonial period produced the paintings of Pérez de Holguín, Flores, Bitti, and others as well as the works of skilled but unknown stonecutters, woodcarvers, goldsmiths, and silversmiths. An important body of Native Baroque religious music of the colonial period was recovered and has been performed internationally to wide acclaim since 1994.[229] Artists of 20th century include María Luisa Pacheco, Roberto Mamani Mamani, Alejandro Mario Yllanes, Alfredo Da Silva, and Marina Núñez del Prado.

Regional folk music is distinctive and varied. The "devil dances" at the annual carnival of Oruro are one of the great folkloric events of South America, as is the lesser known carnival at Tarabuco.[229]

Mediaedit
Main article: Media of Bolivia

The World Press Freedom Index described violent attacks against journalists and censorship in Bolivia.[230]

Sportsedit

Football is popular. The national team is the Bolivia national football team. Racquetball is the second most popular sport in Bolivia as for the results in the Odesur 2018 Games held in Cochabamba.[231][232] Bolivia has won 18 medals at the Pan American Games and 15 of them came from racquetball events, including their only gold medals, won in the Men's Team event in 2019 and 2023, plus a Men's Singles Gold in 2023 by world champion Conrrado Moscoso. Basketball is especially popular and influential in the Potosí Department.[233]

The **demographic characteristics of the population of [Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia "Bolivia")** are known from censuses, with the first census undertaken in 1826 and the most recent in 2024. The [National Institute of Statistics of Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Institute_of_Statistics_of_Bolivia "National Institute of Statistics of Bolivia") (INE) has performed this task since 1950. The population of Bolivia in 2024 reached 11 million for the first time in history. The population density is 11.36 inhabitants per square kilometer, and the overall [life expectancy in Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_life_expectancy "List of countries by life expectancy") at birth is 68.2 years. The population has steadily risen from the late 1800s to the present time. The natural growth rate of the population is positive, which has been a continuing trend since the 1950s; in 2012, Bolivia's [birth rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_rate "Birth rate") continued to be higher than the death rate. Bolivia is in the third stage of [demographic transition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographic_transition "Demographic transition"). In terms of age structure, the population is dominated by the 15–64 segment. The median age of the population is 23.1, and the gender ratio of the total population is 0.99 males per female.

Bolivia is inhabited mostly by [Mestizo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mestizo "Mestizo"), [Quechua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quechua_people "Quechua people") and [Aymara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aymara_people "Aymara people"), while minorities include 37 [indigenous groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples_in_Bolivia "Indigenous peoples in Bolivia") (0.3% average per group). Spanish, [Quechua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quechuan_languages "Quechuan languages"), [Aymara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aymara_language "Aymara language"), [Guarani languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guarani_language "Guarani language"), as well as 34 other native languages are the official languages of Bolivia. Spanish is the most-spoken language (60.7%) within the population. The main religions of Bolivia are the [Catholic Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church "Catholic Church") (81.8%), [Evangelicalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangelicalism "Evangelicalism") (11.5%), and [Protestantism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestantism "Protestantism") (2.6%). There is a [literacy rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literacy "Literacy") of 91.2%. An estimated 7.6% of the country's gross domestic product (GDP) is spent on education. The average monthly household income was [Bs.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivian_boliviano "Bolivian boliviano")1,378 ($293) in 1994. In December 2013 the [unemployment rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unemployment#Measurement "Unemployment") was 3.2% of the working population. The average urbanization rate in Bolivia is 67%.

## Population size and structure

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Demographics_of_Bolivia&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Population size and structure")]

The first true estimate of the population of Bolivia came in 1826, in which 997,427 inhabitants were estimated. This number was calculated from the 1796 census organized by [Francisco Gil de Taboada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_Gil_de_Taboada "Francisco Gil de Taboada"), which consisted of several Bolivian cities.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Bolivia#cite_note-1826pop-4) The first modern census was completed in 1831, and ten have been completed since then. The organizer of Bolivia's censuses has changed throughout the years—[Andrés de Santa Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andr%C3%A9s_de_Santa_Cruz "Andrés de Santa Cruz") (1831), The Bolivian Statistical Office (1835, 1854, 1882), The Bolivian Statistical Commission (1845), The National Immigration Bureau and The Statistics and Geographic Propaganda (1900), and The Department of Statistics and Censuses (1950)—with the INE conducting the census since 1976.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Bolivia#cite_note-1826pop-4) The national census is supposed to be conducted every ten years, however, the 2012 census was late because of "climatic factors and the financing." The 2012 census was conducted on 21 November 2012, in which 10,027,254 inhabitants were in the country. The estimated cost of the census was $50 million.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Bolivia#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Bolivia#cite_note-6)

With a population of 10.0 million in 2012, Bolivia [ranks 87th in the world by population](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_population "List of countries by population").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Bolivia#cite_note-2012pop-7) Its population density is 9.13 inhabitants per square kilometer. The overall [life expectancy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_expectancy "Life expectancy") in Bolivia is 65.4. The [total fertility rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_fertility_rate "Total fertility rate") is 2.87 children per mother. Since 1950, the [World Health Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Health_Organization "World Health Organization") (WHO) estimates the birth rate exceeded the death rate of the country.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Bolivia#cite_note-who-8) The population of Bolivia has been increasing since 1900, and has only had a negative per annum growth rate twice in its history (1835 and 1882). Bolivia is in the third stage of [demographic transition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographic_transition "Demographic transition"). There were 562,461 immigrants in Bolivia in 2012, with the most (40.5%) coming from [Argentina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentina "Argentina").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Bolivia#cite_note-9) In 2008, there were 48,809 marriages in Bolivia, and 5,887 divorces throughout the country in 2011.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Bolivia#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Bolivia#cite_note-11)

The vast majority of Bolivians are [mestizo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mestizo "Mestizo") (with the indigenous component higher than the European one), although the government has not included the cultural self-identification "mestizo" in the November 2012 census.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Bolivia#cite_note-22) There are approximately three dozen native groups totaling approximately half of the Bolivian population – the largest proportion of indigenous people in the Americas. Exact numbers vary based on the wording of the ethnicity question and the available response choices. For example, the 2001 census did not provide the racial category "mestizo" as a response choice, resulting in a much higher proportion of respondents identifying themselves as belonging to one of the available indigenous ethnicity choices. Mestizos are distributed throughout the entire country and make up 26% of the Bolivian population, with the predominantly mestizo departments being Beni, Santa Cruz, and Tarija. Most people assume their _mestizo_ identity while at the same time identifying themselves with one or more indigenous cultures. A 2018 estimate of racial classification put mestizo (mixed white and Amerindian) at 68%, indigenous at 20%, white at 5%, [cholo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cholo#Bolivia "Cholo") at 2%, black at 1%, other at 4%, while 2% were unspecified; 44% attributed themselves to some indigenous group, predominantly the linguistic categories of [Quechuas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quechuas "Quechuas") or [Aymaras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aymara_people "Aymara people").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Bolivia#cite_note-cia-20)[White Bolivians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Latin_Americans "White Latin Americans") comprised about 14% of the population in 2006, and are usually concentrated in the largest cities: [La Paz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Paz "La Paz"), [Santa Cruz de la Sierra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra "Santa Cruz de la Sierra") and [Cochabamba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba "Cochabamba"), but as well in some minor cities like [Tarija](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarija "Tarija") and [Sucre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sucre "Sucre"). The ancestry of whites and the white ancestry of mestizos lies most notably Spain, Italy, Germany, and [Croatia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Croatia "Croatia"). In the [Santa Cruz Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_Department,_Bolivia "Santa Cruz Department, Bolivia"), there are several dozen colonies of German-speaking [Mennonites from Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Mennonite "Russian Mennonite") totaling around 40,000 inhabitants (as of 2012[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Demographics_of_Bolivia&action=edit)).[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Bolivia#cite_note-23)

[Afro-Bolivians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afro-Bolivian "Afro-Bolivian"), descendants of [African slaves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_slave_trade "Atlantic slave trade") who arrived in the time of the [Spanish Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Empire "Spanish Empire"), inhabit the [department of La Paz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Paz_Department,_Bolivia "La Paz Department, Bolivia"), and are located mainly in the provinces of [Nor Yungas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nor_Yungas_Province "Nor Yungas Province") and [Sud Yungas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sud_Yungas_Province "Sud Yungas Province"). Slavery was abolished in Bolivia in 1831.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Bolivia#cite_note-24) There are also important communities of [Japanese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_Bolivians "Japanese Bolivians") (14,000[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Bolivia#cite_note-25)) and Lebanese (12,900[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Bolivia#cite_note-26)).

[Indigenous peoples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Americas "Indigenous peoples of the Americas"), also called _"originarios"_ ("native" or "original") and less frequently, _Amerindians_, could be categorized by geographic area, such as [Andean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes "Andes"), like the [Aymaras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aymara_people "Aymara people") and [Quechuas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quechua_people "Quechua people") (who formed the ancient [Inca Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inca_Empire "Inca Empire")), who are concentrated in the western departments of [La Paz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Paz_Department,_Bolivia "La Paz Department, Bolivia"), [Potosí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD_Department "Potosí Department"), [Oruro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oruro_Department "Oruro Department"), [Cochabamba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba_Department "Cochabamba Department") and [Chuquisaca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department "Chuquisaca Department"). There also are ethnic populations in the east, composed of the [Chiquitano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiquitano "Chiquitano"), [Chané](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chan%C3%A9 "Chané"), [Guaraní](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guaran%C3%AD_people "Guaraní people") and [Moxos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moxo_people "Moxo people"), among others, who inhabit the departments of [Santa Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_Department,_Bolivia "Santa Cruz Department, Bolivia"), [Beni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beni_Department "Beni Department"), [Tarija](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarija_Department "Tarija Department") and [Pando](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pando_Department "Pando Department").

There are small numbers of European citizens from Germany, France, Italy and Portugal, as well as from other countries of the Americas, as Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Cuba, Ecuador, the United States, Paraguay, Peru, Mexico and Venezuela, among others. There are important Peruvian colonies in [La Paz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Paz "La Paz"), [El Alto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Alto "El Alto") and [Santa Cruz de la Sierra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra "Santa Cruz de la Sierra").

There are around 140,000 [Mennonites in Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mennonites_in_Bolivia "Mennonites in Bolivia") of Friesian, Flemish and German ethnic origins.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Bolivia#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Bolivia#cite_note-28)

A few Bolivians carry some Middle Eastern ancestry, mainly from Syria and Lebanon.

The [Indigenous peoples of Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples_of_Bolivia "Indigenous peoples of Bolivia") can be divided into two categories of ethnic groups: the Andeans, who are located in the [Andean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes "Andes")[Altiplano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altiplano "Altiplano") and the valley region; and the lowland groups, who inhabit the warm regions of central and eastern Bolivia, including the valleys of Cochabamba Department, the Amazon Basin areas of northern La Paz Department, and the lowland departments of Beni, Pando, Santa Cruz, and Tarija (including the [Gran Chaco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gran_Chaco "Gran Chaco") region in the southeast of the country). Large numbers of Andean peoples have also migrated to form Quechua, Aymara, and intercultural communities in the lowlands.

*   **Andean ethnicities**
    *   [Aymara people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aymara_people "Aymara people"). They live on the high plateau of the departments of La Paz, Oruro and Potosí, as well as some small regions near the tropical flatlands.
    *   [Quechua people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quechua_people "Quechua people"). They mostly inhabit the valleys in [Cochabamba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba_Department "Cochabamba Department") and [Chuquisaca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuquisaca_Department "Chuquisaca Department"). They also inhabit some mountain regions in [Potosí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potos%C3%AD_Department "Potosí Department") and [Oruro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oruro_Department "Oruro Department"). They divide themselves into different Quechua nations, as the Tarabucos, Ucumaris, Chalchas, Chaquies, Yralipes, Tirinas, among others.
    *   [Uru people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uru_people "Uru people")

*   **Ethnicities of the Eastern Lowlands**
    *   [Guaraníes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guaran%C3%AD_people "Guaraní people"): made up of Guarayos, Pausernas, [Sirionós](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sirion%C3%B3 "Sirionó"), [Chiriguanos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ava_Guaran%C3%AD_people "Ava Guaraní people"), [Wichí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wich%C3%AD "Wichí"), Chulipis, Taipetes, [Tobas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toba_people "Toba people"), and Yuquis.
    *   **Tacanas**: made up of Lecos, Chimanes, Araonas, and Maropas.
    *   **Panos**: made up of Chacobos, Caripunas, Sinabos, Capuibos, and Guacanaguas.
    *   **Aruacos**: made up of Apolistas, Baures, [Moxos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moxo_people "Moxo people"), [Chané](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chan%C3%A9_people "Chané people"), Movimas, Cayabayas, Carabecas, and Paiconecas (Paucanacas).
    *   **Chapacuras**: made up of Itenez (More), Chapacuras, Sansinonianos, Canichanas, Itonamas, Yuracares, Guatoses, and [Chiquitanos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiquitano "Chiquitano").
    *   **Botocudos**: made up of Bororos and Otuquis.
    *   **Zamucos**: made up of [Ayoreos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayoreo_people "Ayoreo people").

PREFACE

The second component consists, once the problem areas of the previous historical account have been identified, in providing new data based on correctly interpreted documents and testimonies. In this way, the rectifying task is associated with the elaboration of new, more solid perspectives, which contribute to the endless effort to generate a true knowledge of the past.It only remains, then, to invite a careful reading of this book that will undoubtedly leave a deep mark on the path of reflection on the background and consequences of the creation of a country as improbable as Bolivia.The first component of historical revisionism consists of the critical analysis of the whole of historiography dedicated to a theme, period or place. Here, what is sought to verify is the solidity of the documents and testimonies that led to establishing dates and facts of the past, as well as the origin and subsequent dissemination of the texts that express them. This aspect of the investigation generally makes it possible to reveal gaps and inaccuracies in the information, eventual attempts to manipulate the data and/or simple errors that, by dint of being repeated, take on all the appearances of the truth.With this background it is possible to ponder the interest of this work by Jorge Hurtado Hervas, who, based on abundant documentation, partially unpublished, proposes a renewed vision of the chaotic birth of Bolivia. Being an investigative work, it is natural that it provokes discussion and a timely confrontation of sources, because only through serious and documented debate will we be able to get closer and closer to the truth of the facts.Historical knowledge, due to its own characteristics, is always in the process of being enriched and revised. Taking this fact into account, it is understood that revisionism is part of the historian's practice itself. In turn, this task is based on two main components.It is that, with few research centers and training of specialized professionals, a large part of Bolivian history suffers from a tendency to repeat supposed truths based on works that, for various reasons, lack the indispensable rigor in terms of historical criticism. . To which is added, in the case of the emancipation process, an ideological bias that leads many authors to assume, at the wrong time, a "patriot" militancy and a propaganda tone that, although it is understandable in the very context of the facts , after two centuries it is absolutely irrelevant. These same observations apply, with much more reason, to the Santa Cruz history of this period, whose critical review is currently beginning.2 In the case of the history of Bolivia in general, and of the history of Santa Cruz in particular, much remains to be done in terms of revisionism, and this is notorious as regards the process of emancipation and creation of the Bolivian "national" State. (1809-1825).Dr Daniel Dory

FOREWORD

First of all, I must point out that my dear friend Jorge Hurtado Hervas is not impromptu in his knowledge of our history. On the contrary, he has been interested in this matter for at least twenty years, as he is the owner in Santa Cruz de la Sierra of one of the most important Archives and Private Library in the region. Books and papers that I have consulted frequently, in the course of some of my historical research.Today I have before me this new document, work and intellectual product that I must analyze and present to the kind reader, a task that is undoubtedly complicated and difficult, due to its subject matter and the novel information that it offers us, which is why I request in advance But before going into the matter, allow me the reader to dedicate a few paragraphs to the author, considering that this will allow us to know some facets of the researcher who gives us this work.However, my friend Jorge, for a long time, had shown concern about the events in Santa Cruz de la Sierra and Vallegrande, specifically on the occasion of the short period of transition from colony to republic, a thematic concern that he later extended to Upper Peru and its process. emancipator. This book is the product of those concerns and the result of more than two years of arduous and sustained research.When commemorating the Bicentennial of the First Libertarian Cry in Santa Cruz de la Sierra, Jorge Hurtado Hervas introduces us to his first historical work, entitled 

“THUS BOLIVIA WAS BORN. THE DIFFICULT PROCESS OF TRANSITION FROM THE COLONY TO THE REPUBLIC”.

**Santa Cruz de la Sierra** (Spanish:[[ˈsanta ˈkɾus ðe la ˈsjera]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish"); lit.'Holy Cross of the Mountain Range'), commonly known as **Santa Cruz**, is the largest city in [Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia "Bolivia") and the capital of the [Santa Cruz department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_Department_(Bolivia) "Santa Cruz Department (Bolivia)").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra#cite_note-autogenerated1-6)

Situated on the [Pirai River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pirai_River_(Bolivia) "Pirai River (Bolivia)") in the eastern Tropical Lowlands of Bolivia, the Santa Cruz de la Sierra Metropolitan Region is the most populous urban agglomeration in Bolivia with an estimated population of 2.4 million[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra#cite_note-7) in 2020. It is formed out of a conurbation of seven Santa Cruz municipalities: Santa Cruz de la Sierra, [La Guardia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Guardia,_Bolivia "La Guardia, Bolivia"), [Warnes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warnes,_Bolivia "Warnes, Bolivia"), [Cotoca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cotoca "Cotoca"), [El Torno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Torno,_Santa_Cruz "El Torno, Santa Cruz"), [Porongo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porongo "Porongo"), and [Montero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montero,_Bolivia "Montero, Bolivia").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra#cite_note-8)

The city was first founded in 1561 by Spanish explorer [Ñuflo de Chavez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%91uflo_de_Chavez "Ñuflo de Chavez") about 200 km (124 mi) east of its current location, and was moved several times until it was finally established on the [Pirai River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piray_River "Piray River") in the late 16th century. For much of its history, Santa Cruz was mostly a small outpost town, and even after Bolivia gained its independence in 1825 there was little attention from the authorities or the population in general to settle the region. It was not until after the middle of the 20th century with profound agrarian and land reforms that the city began to grow at a very fast pace. Due to its low elevation at the foothills of the [Andes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes "Andes") and being situated in the [Amazon basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_basin "Amazon basin"), the city has a [tropical climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra#Climate) unlike the other main metro area of [La Paz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Paz "La Paz") that is thousands of meters higher in terms of elevation.

Santa Cruz is Bolivia's most populous city, produces nearly 35% of Bolivia's [gross domestic product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GDP "GDP"), and receives over 40% of all [foreign direct investment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_direct_investment "Foreign direct investment") in the country. The city is the most important business center in Bolivia and the country's principal destination for national and international migrants.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra#cite_note-9)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Pre-Columbian era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Pre-Columbian era")]

Like much of the history of the people of the region, the history of the area before the arrival of European explorers is not well documented, mostly because of the somewhat nomadic nature and the absence of a [written language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Written_language "Written language") in the culture of the local tribes. However, recent data suggests that the current location of the city of Santa Cruz was inhabited by an [Arawak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arawak "Arawak") tribe that later came to be known by the Spanish as [Chané](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chan%C3%A9 "Chané"). Remains of ceramics and weapons have been found in the area, leading researchers to believe they had established settlements in the area. Among the few known facts of these tribes, according to accounts of the first Spanish explorers that came into contact with the Chané, are that they had a formal leader, a _cacique_, called Grigotá for several years but his reign came to an end after one of the several [Guarani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Bolivian_Guarani "Eastern Bolivian Guarani") (Chiriguano) incursions in the area.

### Early European incursions and founding of the city

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Early European incursions and founding of the city")]

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/Gobernaciones_espa%C3%B1olas_en_Am%C3%A9rica_del_Sur_%281534-1539%29.svg/250px-Gobernaciones_espa%C3%B1olas_en_Am%C3%A9rica_del_Sur_%281534-1539%29.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mapa_de_Am%C3%A9rica_del_Sur_(Gobernaciones_1534-1539).svg)

The _[adelantado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adelantado "Adelantado")_ grants of [Charles V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_V,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor") before the establishment of the [Viceroyalty of Peru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viceroyalty_of_Peru "Viceroyalty of Peru").

The first Europeans to set foot in the area were Spanish [conquistadores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conquistadores "Conquistadores")[_[when?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_] from the recently created [Governorate of New Andalusia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governorate_of_New_Andalusia "Governorate of New Andalusia") that encompassed the territories of present-day Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay, and Chile.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In 1549, Captain General [Domingo Martinez de Irala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domingo_Martinez_de_Irala "Domingo Martinez de Irala") became the first Spaniard to explore the region, but it was not until 1558 that [Ñuflo de Chavez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%91uflo_de_Chaves "Ñuflo de Chaves"), who had arrived in [Asunción](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asunci%C3%B3n "Asunción") in 1541 with [Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%81lvar_N%C3%BA%C3%B1ez_Cabeza_de_Vaca "Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca"), led a new expedition with the objective of settling the region.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] After discovering that a new expedition from Asunción was already underway, he quickly traveled to [Lima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lima "Lima") and successfully persuaded the [Viceroy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viceroy "Viceroy") to create a new province and grant him the title of governor on February 15, 1560.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Upon returning from Lima, Chavez founded the city of Santa Cruz de la Sierra (Holy Cross of the Mountain Range) on February 26, 1561, 220 km (137 mi) east of its present-day location, to function as the capital of the newly formed province of [Moxos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moxos_Province "Moxos Province") and Chaves. The settlement was named after Chaves's [home town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra,_Spain "Santa Cruz de la Sierra, Spain") in [Extremadura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extremadura "Extremadura"), where he grew up before venturing to America.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Shortly after the founding, attacks from local tribes became commonplace and Ñuflo de Chaves was killed in 1568 by Itatine natives. After Chaves's death, the conflicts with the local population as well as power struggles in the settlement forced the authorities in Peru to order the new governor, Lorenzo Suarez de Figueroa to relocate the city to the west. Many of the inhabitants, however, chose to stay behind and continued living in the original location. On September 13, 1590, the city was officially moved to the banks of the Guapay Empero river and renamed San Lorenzo de la Frontera. Nevertheless, the conditions proved to be even more severe at the new location forcing the settlers to relocate once again on May 21, 1595. Although this was the final relocation of the city, the name San Lorenzo continued to be used until the early 17th century, when the settlers who remained behind in Santa Cruz de la Sierra were convinced by the colonial authorities to move to San Lorenzo. After they moved the city was finally consolidated in 1622 and took its original name of Santa Cruz de la Sierra given by Ñuflo de Chaves over 60 years before. Remnants of the original settlement can be visited in Santa Cruz la Vieja ("Old Santa Cruz"), an archaeological site south of San José de Chiquitos.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra#cite_note-11)

### Colonial Santa Cruz and revolutionary war

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Colonial Santa Cruz and revolutionary war")]

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1e/Ignacio_Warnes.jpg/250px-Ignacio_Warnes.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ignacio_Warnes.jpg)

[Ignacio Warnes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ignacio_Warnes "Ignacio Warnes"), the first governor of Santa Cruz

Over the next 200 years, several tribes were either incorporated under Spanish control or defeated by force.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The city also became an important staging point for [Jesuit missions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesuit_reductions "Jesuit reductions") to [Chiquitos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiquitos "Chiquitos") and Moxos, leading to the conversion of thousands of Guaranies, Moxeños, Chiquitanos, [Guarayos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guarayos "Guarayos") and Chiriguanos that eventually became part of the racially mixed population of the modern Santa Cruz, [Beni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beni_Department "Beni Department"), [Pando](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pando_Department "Pando Department") and [Tarija](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarija_Department "Tarija Department") departments of Bolivia. Another important role the small town played in the region for the [Spanish Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Empire "Spanish Empire") was to contain the incursions of Portuguese [Bandeirantes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bandeirantes "Bandeirantes"), many of which were repelled by the use of force over the years.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The efforts for consolidating the borders of the Empire were not overlooked by the authorities in Lima, who granted the province a great degree of autonomy.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The province was ruled by a Captain General based in Santa Cruz, and, in turn, the city government was administered by two mayors and a council of four people. Citizens of Santa Cruz were exempt from all imperial taxes and the [mita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mita_(Inca) "Mita (Inca)") system used in the rest of the [Viceroyalty of Peru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viceroyalty_of_Peru "Viceroyalty of Peru") was not practiced. However, in spite of its strategic importance, the city did not grow much in colonial times. Most of the economic activity was centered in the mining centers of the west and the main source of income of the city was agriculture.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Animosity towards imperial authorities began at the turn of the 18th century when the new system of [intendencias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intendencia#Spanish_monarchy "Intendencia") reached the new world. The seat of government was taken away from the city and moved to [Cochabamba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochabamba "Cochabamba"), and many of the powers delegated by the viceroyalty were now in the hands of appointees of the crown.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Like in many parts of Spanish America at the time, angered by the reforms the criollos saw as a threat to their way of life, and taking advantage of the [Peninsular War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peninsular_War "Peninsular War"), the local population, led by Antonio Vicente Seoane, revolted on September 24, 1810, overthrowing the governor delegate. A junta of local commanders took control of the government in his place. The revolutionaries, as it was the case with most of the revolts in [Spanish America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_America "Spanish America"), remained loyal to the [King of Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_of_Spain "King of Spain"), while repudiating the colonial authorities until after the end of the Peninsular War.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

By 1813 the city was once again under imperial control. At this time, by order of General [Manuel Belgrano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_Belgrano "Manuel Belgrano"), the revolutionary armies of Argentina sent a small force led by [Ignacio Warnes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ignacio_Warnes "Ignacio Warnes") to "liberate" Santa Cruz. After his successful campaign, he assumed control of the government of the city. In a little over a year Warnes was able to gather tremendous support from the population, enlisting criollos, mestizos and natives to the revolutionary army, and allying with the revolutionary leader of [Vallegrande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vallegrande "Vallegrande"), Alvarez de Arenales, to defeat a strong imperial force in the Battle of Florida. This victory proved to be a serious blow to Spanish forces in the region. Nevertheless, two years after the victory of Florida, imperial forces launched a new offensive in the province led by Francisco Javier Aguilera. This campaign ended with the defeat and death of Ignacio Warnes and his forces in the Battle of Pari. Triumphant, Aguilera marched into the city with orders to quell the insurrection and reinstate the Spanish governor. This proved to be a very difficult task, with several revolutionary leaders, such as Jose Manuel "Cañoto" Baca and Jose Manuel Mercado, rising up in the coming years from the city itself and elsewhere in the province. These new leaders fought colonial authorities for seven years until they finally deposed the last Spanish governor, Manuel Fernando Aramburu, in February 1825 after news of the defeat of the imperial armies in the west had reached the city.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra#cite_note-12)

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Geography")]

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e8/SantaCruzBoliviaFromTheISS.jpg/250px-SantaCruzBoliviaFromTheISS.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:SantaCruzBoliviaFromTheISS.jpg)

Santa Cruz, seen from the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station")

The city is located in the eastern part of Bolivia (17°45', South, 63°14', West) at around 400 m above [sea level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_level "Sea level").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra#cite_note-13) It is part of the province of [Andrés Ibáñez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andr%C3%A9s_Ib%C3%A1%C3%B1ez "Andrés Ibáñez") and the capital of the department of Santa Cruz. The city of Santa Cruz is located not far from the easternmost extent of the Andes Mountains and they are visible from some parts of the city.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra#cite_note-14)

### Climate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Climate")]

The city has a [tropical monsoon climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_monsoon_climate "Tropical monsoon climate") ([Köppen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen-Geiger_climate_classification_system "Köppen-Geiger climate classification system"): _Am_), with an average annual temperature around 25°C (77°F) and all months above 18°C or 64.4°F . Santa Cruz is an example of the influence of continentality (reflecting the [thermal amplitude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_temperature#Temperature_range "Atmospheric temperature")) in the [tropics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropics "Tropics"), without the four well-defined seasons of the year but greater deviations of temperature than other places in the coast or island.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra#cite_note-16) Although the weather is generally very warm all year round, cold winds called "surazos" can blow in occasionally (particularly in the winter) from the Argentine [pampas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pampas "Pampas") making the temperature drop considerably. The months of greatest rainfall are December and January. The average annual rainfall is 1,321 mm (52 in).[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra#cite_note-17) Santa Cruz sits at the edge of the Codo de Arica, where winds are particularly strong in Bolivia. Annual variations in temperature and precipitation are common, as is the case across much of the region. Annual precipitation in recent history has varied between 900 and 2,300 millimetres (35 and 91 in).

## Demographics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Demographics")]

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9a/VistaSC.jpg/250px-VistaSC.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:VistaSC.jpg)

Aerial view of Santa Cruz de la Sierra

The city of Santa Cruz is, besides being the largest city in [Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia "Bolivia"), the one with the greatest mestizo and Creole identity, and with a smaller indigenous population. The first settlers of Santa Cruz were mainly the Native [Chane people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chane_people "Chane people") of East Bolivia followed by the Spaniards that accompanied Ñuflo de Chávez, as well as [Guarani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guarani_people "Guarani people") natives from [Paraguay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paraguay "Paraguay"), and other native American groups that previously lived there working for the Spanish crown. Eventually, the Spanish settlers and native people of Bolivia began to mix which has resulted in the majority of the city population being [mestizo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mestizo "Mestizo"). When the Spanish settlers arrived to Bolivia, [Catholicism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholicism "Catholicism"), as well as the Spanish language, were implemented onto the natives which is now why the city is predominantly Catholic and speaks Spanish. Nevertheless, native religions and languages are still used by a minority of the population.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra#cite_note-22)

There was a distinction between the ethno-demographic profile of the Santa Cruz de la Sierra region, marked by the mestizo, Spanish and eastern indigenous presence, in relation to the population of the Bolivian Altiplano, western part of the country mostly Andean indigenous with a smaller mestizo and Spanish presence. However, in the last 60 years, large migrations from the western regions of Bolivia to Santa Cruz have transformed the demographics of the city and department redefining its social and ethnic spectrum.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra#cite_note-23) In recent years, external migration has also become noticeable in Santa Cruz. Immigrants in Bolivia, especially in Santa Cruz have mainly originated from [Argentina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentina "Argentina"), [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil "Brazil"), [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain"), [Peru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peru "Peru"), [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") and [Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico "Mexico").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra#cite_note-24)

## Economy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Economy")]

[![Image 26](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0b/Zona_Equipetrol%2C_Santa_Cruz.jpg/250px-Zona_Equipetrol%2C_Santa_Cruz.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Zona_Equipetrol,_Santa_Cruz.jpg)

[Equipetrol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equipetrol?action=edit&redlink=1 "Equipetrol (page does not exist)") Neighborhood

Santa Cruz de la Sierra is Bolivia's main economic, commercial, and industrial center. Its economy is divided into several specialized sectors, including entertainment, gastronomy, textiles, banking, agroindustry, tourism, automotive, and other industries.

Following its development and economic exposure, the city has the highest Human Development Index ([HDI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Development_Index "Human Development Index")) in the country, with a value of 0.827 at the city level and 0.758 at the department level.

Its population growth is among the fastest in the [Americas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Americas "Americas").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra#cite_note-25) It has a nominal [GDP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GDP "GDP") of $9.175 billion, a nominal GDP per capita of just over $4,200, and a PPP GDP per capita of $12,800.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra#cite_note-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra#cite_note-27)

It is also considered the franchise capital of Bolivia, as it has the largest number of national and international franchises in the country, spanning various categories, such as [Hard Rock Cafe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_Rock_Cafe "Hard Rock Cafe"), [Starbucks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starbucks "Starbucks"), [Kentucky Fried Chicken](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kentucky_Fried_Chicken "Kentucky Fried Chicken"), [Pizza Hut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pizza_Hut "Pizza Hut"), [Juan Valdez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Valdez "Juan Valdez"), [Cinemark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinemark "Cinemark"), [Sbarro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sbarro "Sbarro"), [Carl's Jr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl's_Jr "Carl's Jr"), [Subway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subway_(restaurant) "Subway (restaurant)"), [Burger King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burger_King "Burger King"), [T.G.I. Santa Cruz de la Sierra has consolidated its position as Bolivia's main real estate center in recent years, driven by its population growth, which will exceed three million by 2024,[_[needs update](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_] and by the arrival of internal migrants. The high proportion of young people, representing more than 60% of the population,[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra#cite_note-28) has boosted demand for apartments and high-rise buildings, replacing traditional housing.

Between 2020 and 2023, more than one million square meters were built annually,[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra#cite_note-29) and in 2023, 51 towers of ten floors or more were registered, reaching a total of 261.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra#cite_note-30) Growth was especially concentrated in District 5, with nearly 43% of construction licenses. In the same year, an average of 399 properties were sold per month, compared to 285 in 2022, with a predominance of cash transactions.

Although the sector faces higher material costs and a slowdown in projections (estimated between 0.5% and 1.5% annually),[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra#cite_note-31) it continues to be one of the main drivers of investment in the city, supported by the expansion of the middle class and Santa Cruz's role as the country's economic capital.

The main facade of the [Cathedral Basilica of San Lorenzo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cathedral_Basilica_of_St._Lawrence,_Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra "Cathedral Basilica of St. Lawrence, Santa Cruz de la Sierra"), built in 1595.

Santa Cruz de la Sierra welcomes a third of the country's domestic tourists, plus a small amount of international tourism. Some of the attractions in and around the city include:

*   [Metropolitan Cathedral Basilica of San Lorenzo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cathedral_Basilica_of_St._Lawrence,_Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra "Cathedral Basilica of St. Lawrence, Santa Cruz de la Sierra") was built by Friar Diego de Porres during the reign of the Spanish Viceroy Toledo. In 1770, Bishop Ramón de Herbosos rebuilt the church, entrusting the execution of the works to the chief sacristan Antonio Lombardo. During the reign of Marshal [Andrés de Santa Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andr%C3%A9s_de_Santa_Cruz "Andrés de Santa Cruz") (1838), the old temple was replaced by a new eclectic-style church, designed by the French architect Felipe Bestres. It is notable for its wooden vaults and the pictorial decoration that covers them. Part of the original carved silver covering from the Jesuit mission of San Pedro de Moxos is preserved on the high altar. Four sculptural reliefs from the same mission are also on display.
*   Plaza 24 de Septiembre: Several blocks around the main plaza, 24 de Septiembre, are colonial-style buildings. Here you'll find the House of Culture, the Departmental Prefecture, the Municipal Mayor's Office, the Metropolitan Cathedral, several interesting museums, and exhibition halls.

[![Image 38](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9f/Lomas_de_Arena_-_Santa_Cruz%2C_Bolivia.jpg/250px-Lomas_de_Arena_-_Santa_Cruz%2C_Bolivia.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lomas_de_Arena_-_Santa_Cruz,_Bolivia.jpg)

The Lomas de Arena

Its beauty is comparable to [beaches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beach "Beach") due to the color of its sand.
*   Monseñor Rivero Avenue, a pleasant boulevard in the city, is home to entertainment venues, including restaurants, cafes, ice cream parlors, and pastry shops.
*   Playland amusement park
*   The [Noel Kempff Mercado South American Fauna Zoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noel_Kempff_Mercado_Municipal_Zoo_of_South_American_Fauna?action=edit&redlink=1 "Noel Kempff Mercado Municipal Zoo of South American Fauna (page does not exist)") is an exclusive tropical wildlife reserve with semi-wild specimens, including unique species such as the [spectacled bear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectacled_bear "Spectacled bear") (jucumari), the [sloth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sloth "Sloth"), multicolored macaws, jaguars, and other species.
*   [Carnaval Cruceño](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra_Carnival?action=edit&redlink=1 "Santa Cruz de la Sierra Carnival (page does not exist)"): It is one of the most popular and colorful celebrations in Bolivia, especially in the [eastern part of the country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivian_East?action=edit&redlink=1 "Bolivian East (page does not exist)"). It is characterized by its festive atmosphere, lively [comparsas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comparsa_(carnival)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Comparsa (carnival) (page does not exist)"), float parades, and the election of the [Carnival Queen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annex:Queens_of_the_Santa_Cruz_Carnival?action=edit&redlink=1 "Annex:Queens of the Santa Cruz Carnival (page does not exist)"), the central figure of the celebration.

The Güembé Biocenter, a 24-hectare nature reserve that houses exotic flora and fauna typical of the region.

*   Güembé Biocenter, La Rinconada, and the Yvaga Guazú Ecological Park, among others. All are important centers or complexes for natural delights and ecological trails. The first features a large number of natural-style pools with lagoons and walkways through a butterfly house and a large aviary with a large ecological viewing platform. The second is a place filled with nature, lush gardens, lagoons, and a pool. The third is filled with vegetation, green trails, and wild animals all around.
*   The city also attracts people from all over the world for cosmetic surgery due to its low cost.
*   Cabañas del Río Piraí: Located in the western part of the capital, at the end of Roca and Coronado Avenues, they offer beautiful views of the riverbanks. The cabins offer delicious traditional dishes. The Piraí River is a popular spot on hot days. You can also go horseback riding or ATV riding along the river beaches, and enjoy tarpon net fishing from March to June.

### Architecture and urban planning

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Architecture and urban planning")]

[![Image 40](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f0/Vista_a%C3%A9rea_de_Scz-Bolivia.jpg/250px-Vista_a%C3%A9rea_de_Scz-Bolivia.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Vista_a%C3%A9rea_de_Scz-Bolivia.jpg)

The city has a radial urban layout.

[![Image 41](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cf/Edificios_en_Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra%2C_Bolivia.jpg/250px-Edificios_en_Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra%2C_Bolivia.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Edificios_en_Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra,_Bolivia.jpg)

Historic buildings around the city center.

From an urban planning perspective, the city center is delimited by a main network of streets laid out in the traditional Spanish style, which organized the space in [similar blocks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hippodamian_plan "Hippodamian plan"), locating the main religious, government, and economic buildings around a central plaza. This sector in Santa Cruz constitutes the "old town," structured around the [main square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plaza_24_de_Septiembre?action=edit&redlink=1 "Plaza 24 de Septiembre (page does not exist)") or main square. After this central block, the [ring network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra_Rings?action=edit&redlink=1 "Santa Cruz de la Sierra Rings (page does not exist)") begins. A road system of surrounding avenues, from which other avenues called "radials" branch off, dispersing in multiple directions. The city is made up of 10 concentric ring roads, each 1 to 2 km apart, and 27 radial roads that branch off from the first ring road and cross the entire city. The city was planned to have four ring roads by 2000, but given the city's rapid population growth, many peripheral neighborhoods affected the layout of the rings above the fourth. The location of the Piraí River (Bolivia) is the natural limit for the layout of some rings.

The city has experienced significant growth in road traffic; related projects include a tunnel under the El Trompillo Airport runway, which connected the interrupted section of the fourth ring road in the southern part of the city. Another important work is the overpasses at the intersections of the 4th, 5th, 6th and 7th ring roads with Av. Cristo Redentor, among others.

### Parks and gardens

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Parks and gardens")]

[![Image 42](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2a/Jard%C3%ADn_Bot%C3%A1nico_de_Santa_Cruz.jpg/250px-Jard%C3%ADn_Bot%C3%A1nico_de_Santa_Cruz.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jard%C3%ADn_Bot%C3%A1nico_de_Santa_Cruz.jpg)

The Botanical Garden of Santa Cruz de la Sierra

The largest parks in Santa Cruz are located in the city's different districts and are known as Urban Parks. Several of these parks are surrounded by fences for security. In the city center is [Parque El Arenal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parque_El_Arenal?action=edit&redlink=1 "Parque El Arenal (page does not exist)"), which stands out for its lagoon and island, and also serves as the area's rainwater reservoir. This park is home to Lorgio Vaca's mural. Along the city's first ring road, a series of trees have been planted, converting the central median into a garden with a promenade. A little further out, between Avenida Argentina and the second, is [Central Urban Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parque_Urbano_Central_de_Santa_Cruz?action=edit&redlink=1 "Parque Urbano Central de Santa Cruz (page does not exist)"), where sports activities are possible. It is decorated with dinosaurs and has dancing fountains where different types of music play and the waters move to the rhythm of the song. Other notable parks are the park outside the [El Trompillo Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Trompillo_Airport "El Trompillo Airport"), which also has dancing waters, the Blacutt square and the [General Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_General_Cemetery?action=edit&redlink=1 "Santa Cruz General Cemetery (page does not exist)"). On the second ring road in the northeast there is a small park that houses the [Pirate Plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pirate_Plane?action=edit&redlink=1 "Pirate Plane (page does not exist)"), which is a [Lockheed Constellation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_Constellation "Lockheed Constellation") aircraft seized by the [Bolivian Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivian_Air_Force "Bolivian Air Force") and converted into a tourist attraction. Already on the outskirts of the city, on the avenue to [Cotoca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cotoca "Cotoca"), is the [Botanical Garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra_Botanical_Garden?action=edit&redlink=1 "Santa Cruz de la Sierra Botanical Garden (page does not exist)"), which has about 500 cataloged species of flora and another 1,000 varieties yet to be cataloged.

## Culture

[![Image 43](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/Vestimenta_Camba.jpg/250px-Vestimenta_Camba.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Vestimenta_Camba.jpg)

Camba clothing, typical of the eastern plains and the department of Santa Cruz

The culture of the department and city of Santa Cruz is of [mestizo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mestizo "Mestizo") origin, with mostly [Spanish, European](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creole_peoples "Creole peoples") contributions and others of indigenous origin, from the [Guarani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guaran%C3%AD_people "Guaraní people"), [Chiquitanos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiquitano_people "Chiquitano people"), and from the Amazon ([Arawaks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arawaks "Arawaks")).[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra#cite_note-32)

### Carnival

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Carnival")]

Main article: [Santa Cruz de la Sierra Carnival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra_Carnival?action=edit&redlink=1 "Santa Cruz de la Sierra Carnival (page does not exist)")

The preparations for the Santa Cruz de la Sierra Carnival begin in December, two to three months beforehand, with its famous pre-Carnival parades, followed by the three-day holiday where people dance in the comparsas or groups formed by these groups, who celebrate in style in large parking lots where they organize to have international and national artists offer massive parties. There's also a stroll through the city center for a more popular, village-based carnival.

### Dances

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Dances")]

In Santa Cruz de la Sierra, it is common to see dances from throughout the department and other regions of the country, as well as international folklore.

The city's most distinctive traditional dances are: the [carnavalito](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnavalito "Carnavalito") cruceño, the brincao, the [chovena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chovena?action=edit&redlink=1 "Chovena (page does not exist)"), the [taquirari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taquirari?action=edit&redlink=1 "Taquirari (page does not exist)"), and the sarao.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra#cite_note-33)

### Urban transportation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Urban transportation")]

[![Image 47](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d0/Avenida_San_Martin%2C_Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra.jpg/250px-Avenida_San_Martin%2C_Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Avenida_San_Martin,_Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra.jpg)

San Martín Avenue connects the 2nd and 3rd rings of the city.

The public transportation system includes buses that travel throughout the city on 132 routes. The service is privatized and managed by the Santa Cruz Bus and Collective Union. The poor administration and route planning are what most harm the city's traffic flow.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra#cite_note-37)

The best-known buses are the so-called "vuelteros" (buses that run along the city's various ring roads). They are named after typical animals from the province to identify the lines (e.g., Chuturubí (_[Pepsis Limbata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pepsis\_Limbata "Pepsis Limbata")_) vueltero on the 1st ring road ([RN7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RN7_(Bolivia) "RN7 (Bolivia)")) and Tiluchi (_[Rufous hornero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rufous\_hornero "Rufous hornero")_) vueltero on the 2nd ring road ([RN9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RN9_(Bolivia) "RN9 (Bolivia)"))).[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra#cite_note-39)

## Sports

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Sports")]

Two of Bolivia's biggest [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football") clubs are located in Santa Cruz de la Sierra: [Club Blooming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Club_Blooming "Club Blooming") and [Oriente Petrolero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oriente_Petrolero "Oriente Petrolero"). Both teams currently play in the [Bolivian Primera División](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivian_Primera_Divisi%C3%B3n "Bolivian Primera División"). The match between the two, known as the [Clásico Cruceño](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cl%C3%A1sico_Cruce%C3%B1o "Clásico Cruceño"), is one of the fiercest rivalries in Bolivia. Each team has won 5 national titles.

Other football teams in Santa Cruz include [Destroyers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Club_Destroyers "Club Destroyers"), [Real Santa Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Santa_Cruz "Real Santa Cruz"), [Royal Pari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Pari_F.C. "Royal Pari F.C."), and [Universidad Cruceña](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Club_Deportivo_Universidad_Cruce%C3%B1a "Club Deportivo Universidad Cruceña").

The main stadium in Santa Cruz is [Estadio Ramón Tahuichi Aguilera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Ram%C3%B3n_Tahuichi_Aguilera "Estadio Ramón Tahuichi Aguilera"). The stadium hosted several matches of the [1997 Copa America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_Copa_America "1997 Copa America") including one of the semi-finals. The stadium is also scheduled to host the final of the [2025 Copa Sudamericana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Copa_Sudamericana "2025 Copa Sudamericana").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra#cite_note-40)

**Santa Cruz de la Sierra** (Spanish:[[ˈsanta ˈkɾus ðe la ˈsjera]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish"); lit.'Holy Cross of the Mountain Range'), commonly known as **Santa Cruz**, is the largest city in [Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia "Bolivia") and the capital of the [Santa Cruz department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_Department_(Bolivia) "Santa Cruz Department (Bolivia)").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra#cite_note-autogenerated1-6)

Situated on the [Pirai River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pirai_River_(Bolivia) "Pirai River (Bolivia)") in the eastern Tropical Lowlands of Bolivia, the Santa Cruz de la Sierra Metropolitan Region is the most populous urban agglomeration in Bolivia with an estimated population of 2.4 million[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra#cite_note-7) in 2020. It is formed out of a conurbation of seven Santa Cruz municipalities: Santa Cruz de la Sierra, [La Guardia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Guardia,_Bolivia "La Guardia, Bolivia"), [Warnes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warnes,_Bolivia "Warnes, Bolivia"), [Cotoca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cotoca "Cotoca"), [El Torno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Torno,_Santa_Cruz "El Torno, Santa Cruz"), [Porongo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porongo "Porongo"), and [Montero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montero,_Bolivia "Montero, Bolivia").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra#cite_note-8)

The city was first founded in 1561 by Spanish explorer [Ñuflo de Chavez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%91uflo_de_Chavez "Ñuflo de Chavez") about 200 km (124 mi) east of its current location, and was moved several times until it was finally established on the [Pirai River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piray_River "Piray River") in the late 16th century. For much of its history, Santa Cruz was mostly a small outpost town, and even after Bolivia gained its independence in 1825 there was little attention from the authorities or the population in general to settle the region. It was not until after the middle of the 20th century with profound agrarian and land reforms that the city began to grow at a very fast pace. Due to its low elevation at the foothills of the [Andes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes "Andes") and being situated in the [Amazon basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_basin "Amazon basin"), the city has a [tropical climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra#Climate) unlike the other main metro area of [La Paz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Paz "La Paz") that is thousands of meters higher in terms of elevation.

Santa Cruz is Bolivia's most populous city, produces nearly 35% of Bolivia's [gross domestic product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GDP "GDP"), and receives over 40% of all [foreign direct investment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_direct_investment "Foreign direct investment") in the country. The city is the most important business center in Bolivia and the country's principal destination for national and international migrants.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra#cite_note-9)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Pre-Columbian era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Santa_Cruz_de_la_Sierra&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Pre-Columbian era")]

[![Image 21: icon](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/99/Question_book-new.svg/60px-Question_book-new.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Question_book-new.svg)This section **does not [cite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources") any [sources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")**.
